Subject: RFI follow-up: retention scopes and PHI redaction

Jonas / Marissa —

Thanks for the quick demo last week. Our RFP team has a couple of follow-ups specifically around data retention and archival for PHI-containing artifacts. High level asks:

1) A table of retention windows by artifact type (conversation transcripts, embeddings, audit logs, KV cache snapshots).
2) Whether you support automatic redaction (PII/PHI) at ingestion and/or at rest, and how that affects analytics and embeddings.
3) Proof that data deletions are irreversible for customer-requested purges (legal/regulatory requirement).
4) Availability of tamper-evident audit logs and the retention/exports for e-discovery.

Can you provide a short technical response and a proposed timeline for inclusion in our procurement packet?

Thanks — Diana

Diana —

Appreciate the clear list. Attaching an initial matrix (Redwood_PHIdata_retention_table.xlsx) that maps artifact types to recommended retention windows and purge controls. High-level answers below; Aditya is adding technical detail on encryption and audit logs.

Summary (short answers):
- Conversation transcripts: default 180 days, configurable down to 0 days with immediate purge API.
- Embeddings (customer-indexed): default 365 days; we can store encrypted embeddings with an optional automatic one-way hashing step to make reversible reconstruction harder.
- Audit logs (auth/access/traces): default 7 years (per enterprise policy), immutable once written; exportable in CSV/JSON for e-discovery.
- KV cache snapshots: ephemeral by default (24–72 hours), configurable persistent snapshots with customer-managed retention.

Redaction:
- Ingestion-time PII/PHI detection: yes (rule + ML hybrid); available as a pipeline that can redact or substitute tokens before storage.
- At-rest redaction: supported via configurable redaction templates; note that redaction will alter downstream embeddings/analytics and we provide a redaction-aware embedding pipeline to re-generate embeddings after redaction.

Purge guarantees:
- Customer-initiated purge triggers an asynchronous workflow that removes primary copies and tombstones secondary replicas; we provide a purge report and cryptographic deletion proof (HMAC-signed manifest) once job completes.

Next steps: we can produce a more formal, itemized response for your procurement packet by Thurs (2027-06-03). If a BAA or alternate retention window is required we can include suggested language for the MSA/BAA.

Diana / team —

Following up with the technical assumptions and options so the procurement/security reviewers have what they need. Key points:

Encryption and KMS:
- All customer data at rest is AES-256 encrypted. For Lifespan we recommend BYOK (bring-your-own-key) using our KMS integration (AWS KMS / Azure Key Vault / GCP KMS) or an HSM-backed service.
- Separate key hierarchies for live serving data vs. long-term archives; customer can rotate keys on demand. Key rotation triggers re-encryption for active shards; archived blobs are re-wrapped.

Audit logs and immutability:
- Audit logs are written to an append-only ledger stored in WORM-enabled object storage. Logs are tamper-evident: each batch includes a SHA-256 chain-of-hashes and we can provide signed manifests for e-discovery.
- Exports are available via S3-compatible exports or secure link; we also support SOC 2-aligned report exports.

Purge mechanics and evidence of deletion:
- Purge job stages: (1) mark records for deletion, (2) remove from live datastore and indexes, (3) remove encrypted blobs from cold storage; (4) rotate keys for any snapshots containing the data if requested.
- We provide a purge manifest signed with our service key and a hash of the removed object IDs. For highly regulated workflows we can optionally run a NIST 800-88 compliant crypto-erase and provide attestation.

De-identification and re-identification risk management:
- We provide both deterministic tokenization and statistical de-identification (k-anonymity approximations) as configured pipelines. We recommend a hybrid approach: tokenization for PHI fields, ML-based redaction for free text.
- Note: embeddings derived from PHI can leak signal. For high-risk workloads we offer a hashed-embeddings mode where embeddings are salted with a per-customer secret; salted embeddings are not reversible without the secret.

Operational controls and SLA impacts:
- Shorter retention windows and aggressive redaction increase compute (reindexing, re-embedding) and may affect throughput/SLOs; we can provide cost+latency delta estimates once you confirm expected QPS and average sequence lengths.

Let me know if you want a short table enumerating API endpoints for purge, redaction, and audit export. I can deliver that in the formal RFI response on Thurs.

Attached is the finalized RFI package tailored for Lifespan: a detailed retention matrix, our redaction spec (redaction_spec_v1.pdf), and the dataflow diagram. Highlights and immediate answers for procurement:

- We can commit to configurable retention windows down to immediate purge for conversation transcripts and embeddings (note: immediate purge will remove records from serving indexes within 2–6 minutes and fully complete across replicas within 24 hours, with a signed purge manifest).
- Audit log retention is configurable; we recommend 7 years by default but can be set per contract. Export and sealed-manifest capabilities are compatible with most e-discovery workflows.
- BAA: we have standard BAA language we can share; for Lifespan-specific exceptions (e.g., minimum audit retention) we can draft contract language.

Proposed next steps:
1) Review attached package and confirm any requested retention deltas by Mon 2027-06-07.
2) If acceptable, we will provide a BAA draft and a DocuSign link for signature within 2 business days of confirmation.
3) Security team (Aditya) can schedule a technical walkthrough and provide an environment-level demo for your engineers.

If you want, I can convert the retention matrix into your template and upload to the procurement portal.

Thanks — looking forward to closing the packet.
